Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB180.xml). Northern Travels Collection of Chan Master Hongjue Min of Tiantong. In an audience with the emperor, an unnamed court scholar asks Muchen Daomin how to work with a Chan question. Muchen says that earlier teachers gave beginners an apparently meaningless question to press against, like an iron wall, until one can no longer turn it this way or that; a person might then neglect sleep and forget meals. The scholar asks how to reach that state. Muchen replies with the selected clause: missing sleep and meals is not something to force. When the scholar has an urgent matter on his mind, he says, he will find that he cannot stop thinking of it. Senses.PreferredTarget: Where there is a place of honor, know the person worthy of honor
AlternateTargets: If there is an honored station, discern the honored person
SearchAliases: where there is a place of honor know the person worthy of honor
Senses.Note: Wangshan Ti says that when there is a position of honor one must know the person worthy of honor. His next sentence says that such a person does not dwell in that position. Later masters probe the distinction between a recognized station and a person who cannot be confined to ranks; several answer him with their own verse or a sharp counter question.

Senses.Explanation: "Where there is a place of honor, know the person worthy of honor" opens Wangshan Ti's teaching on station and person. Its next line says that the person does not dwell in the position. Sanyi and Huigong turn the inherited saying into a challenge about whether any display of honor really shows the person. Baiyu asks for an answer beyond the distinction, Hansong writes a verse, and Suru challenges Wangshan for leaving listeners in ranks.

Senses.Explanation: Perfection is the inherited technical term retained in named compounds. The expository witness says that form is the form of reality's nature: because it has no fixed shape it is called empty, and because knowledge and vision are inexhaustible it is called form. It therefore says that the Tathagata's form is inexhaustible and that wisdom is likewise. Wherever phenomena arise there are innumerable gates of absorption; freedom from inner and outer views and attachments is also called a retention gate and a giving gate. Not entertaining inner or outer, good or bad phenomena, and the further items named there are all gates of perfection. Occurrences.Kwic: 處州龍泉吳氏子。自幼卓犖不凡，早歲慕出世法。年二十三棄家，首造靈石妙，繼見大慧杲於徑山。慧陞堂，稱蔣山應庵為人俓捷。師聞之，不待旦而行。既至，入室，朝夕咨請。一日，庵問：世尊有密語：迦葉不覆藏。汝作麼生？師曰：鈍置和尚。庵勵聲一喝，師有省。庵大喜，以為法器，說偈勸使祝髮。宋隆興初，得度於臨安白蓮。自是徧參諸大老，罕當其意者。廼入閩見木庵永，永舉：有句無句，如藤倚樹。問師，師曰：裂破。永曰：瑯琊道：好一堆爛柴聻。師曰：矢上加尖。永曰：觀公下語，老僧不能過。其如未在，他日拂柄在手，為人不得，騐人不得。師曰：為人者，使博地凡夫一超入聖域固難矣。󳮱人者，打向面前過，不待開口已知渠骨髓，何難之有？永舉手曰：明明向汝道：開口不在舌頭上。後當自知。逾年，見密庵於衢之西山，隨問即答，密庵微笑而已。師切於究竟，至忘寢食。密庵移蔣山、華嚴、徑山，師皆從之。一日，密庵挂牌為眾入室次，問僧：不是心，不是佛，不是物。師侍側，豁然大悟，乃曰：今日方會木庵道：開口不在舌頭上。自是機辯縱橫。密庵遷靈隱，師遂分座。旋出世於平江澄照，徙江陰之光孝、無為之冶父、饒之薦福、明之香山、平江之虎丘。慶元丁巳，被旨補靈隱。

Senses.Explanation: Separation and subtlety form a paired boundary that speech and silence alike can enter. Chan speakers ask how to pass without violating it, demand a phrase that does not fall into it, and describe repeated affirmation and negation as tracks that must be exhausted before the pair can even be discussed. Juelang Daosheng turns a supervisor's practical proposal into the question ‘speech and silence involve separation and subtlety—how can one pass without violating them?’ (語默涉離微，如何通不犯). The same question becomes a recurring public-interview formula in the records of Feiyin Tongrong and Wanru Tongwei. Fushi Tongxian asks for a phrase that does not fall into the pair; Ruibai Mingxue asks how such a phrase is presented. Wuyi Yuanlai places separation and subtlety (離微) after a chain in which teaching, non-teaching, and their negations have left no trace.

Senses.Note: The exact relational phrase is supported by seven distinct uses across seven works. Repeated recensions of the Shanhui verse and Huizhong exchange are counted once, and every occurrence of the larger mind-consciousness formula or a longer boundary crossing is excluded.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「離心一著如何參？」師曰：「繡針眼裏打鞦韆。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB369.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhe'an Jingfan. Speaker: an unnamed monk.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The complete public exchange identifies Zhe'an Jingfan as respondent but does not name the monk who utters the headword. The monk asks how to investigate the 'apart-from-mind move'; Zhe'an answers with swinging inside an embroidery needle's eye.

Senses.Explanation: In these records, 'apart from mind' marks a separation that the speakers deny, condemn as an outside search, or turn into a public test. Shanhui Dashi's paired verse says there is no Buddha apart from mind and no mind apart from Buddha. Nanyang Huizhong condemns seeking Buddha separately from mind, while Changqing Da'an answers a public question by locating Buddha not apart from the ground of mind. Lingyin Qingsong applies the same relation to liberation. Chuiwan Guangzhen's verse says learning the Way does not depart from mind. Jianlong Fayin and Zhe'an Jingfan turn the phrase itself into a bodily and verbal public test.

Entries.SourceTerm: 離心意識參，絕凡聖路學

Senses.PreferredTarget: Investigate beyond mind, intention, and consciousness; learn beyond the paths of ordinary and holy
AlternateTargets: Inquiry must leave mind, thought, and consciousness; study must leave the ordinary and sacred tracks
SearchAliases: leave mind intention consciousness to investigate
Senses.Note: The saying tells a practitioner to investigate without relying on the usual stream of thoughts and discriminations, and to learn without setting ordinary and holy up as two tracks. Masters press students on what this actually requires; repeating the line is not itself the work.

Senses.Explanation: Investigate beyond mind, intention, and consciousness; learn beyond the paths of ordinary and holy gives two linked demands for Chan inquiry. Baishan states the pair to his hall, then tests a monk who asks where to begin. Faxi Yin gives it in instruction to a monastery officer and insists that inquiry and awakening be genuine. Wanru joins it to impossible actions, then says inquiry must reach the point where there is no inquiry. Sanyi opens a hall instruction with it and follows with startling images rather than a conceptual definition. Shanyi says the old line is apt but asks students what they will investigate and learn. Konggu uses it in an extended appeal for sustained inquiry.

Senses.Note: The expression pairs outward appearance with its assigned label. It can describe a clarity that eludes both, yet several masters warn against turning that freedom into a final formula.

Senses.Explanation: To be free of forms and names is to elude both what appears and the labels attached to it. Zhongfeng asks who does not share this freedom, then questions why teachers still divide what is given. Eryin answers a monk’s question with an image of light that is beyond form and name yet dark as lacquer. Baiyu calls the matter originally free of both and asks who could claim to cultivate or attain it. Hanxiu pairs the phrase with freedom from ordinary and holy categories. Jingting says that even reaching this point can still leave a person caught. Miyun’s verse says it becomes fully apparent under a decisive blow. Juelang says practitioners must break through a hard point beyond forms and names rather than merely speak about it.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the proverb says that a hungry person does not pick and choose food. Shending Hongyin uses it as an answer about his house style, and Pang Yun turns it into an oblique reply when Danxia asks whether he is present. Liu Mingxiao's preface supplies the semantic control: 'the hungry do not choose food; once full, they immediately stop.' The image therefore concerns immediate, nonselective uptake under need, but it does not praise endless accumulation; satisfaction marks its limit.

Senses.Explanation: Eating rice when hungry recurs as an answer, self-description, quotation, and point of public criticism, usually paired with sleeping when tired. Huanglong Huinan places it in a four-action series: eat when hungry, sleep when tired, approach fire when cold, and take coolness when hot. Dahui Zonggao quotes Lingzhao’s reply, ‘neither hard nor easy—when hungry, eat rice; when tired, sleep,’ and appraises the Pang family as walking together but not in step. Yuanwu Keqin uses a graphic variant beside ordinary mind, and Dongshan Zhiqian uses it in a self-description. Dazhu Huihai supplies the decisive contrast: other people refuse simply to eat or sleep and instead make a hundred demands and a thousand calculations. Hongzhi Zhengjue likewise says the monastery manager knows only eating when hungry and does not know the many kinds of affairs. The ordinary meal becomes interview language, but the records prevent mere repetition from settling the matter.
